name: Iseult

attributes.attribute: a Cornish or Breton heroine bound to her lover Tristan by a love potion
wife of King Mark of Cornwall, who subjected her to a magical test of purity
the Celtic motif of the goddess who chooses the king, which commentators find in the tale of Iseult

sources: Bedier, Joseph. The Romance of Tristan and Iseult. Translated by Hilaire Belloc. New York: Vintage Books, 1965.
Markale, Jean. Courtly Love: The Path of Sexual Initiation. Rochester, Vt.: Inner Traditions, 2000, 77.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Iseult is a Cornish or Breton heroine. The great romance pairs her with her lover Tristan. Her husband King Mark stands in opposition. The tale parallels the British love triangle of Guinevere, Lancelot, and Arthur. Mark was king of Cornwall. He found a single strand of golden hair. He fell in love with the woman from whose head it came. He sent his nephew Tristan to Ireland to find her. On the return voyage Iseult offered Tristan a drink. Her mother had brewed it for the wedding night. She used arcane herbal knowledge to make a potion. The potion caused intense and boundless love. She meant to assure her daughter's happiness. Instead she destroyed it. Iseult was bound to Tristan from the moment they shared the drink. She did not yield to him physically. She continued her journey and became the bride of Mark. Her maid Brangien took her place in bed on the honeymoon. Brangien felt guilt for having served the potion. Eventually Iseult had to do her wifely duties. She met Tristan in secret. Mark subjected her to a magical test of purity. She had to cross a stream that would drown her if she were impure. Tristan arrived disguised as a beggar and helped her cross. She could honestly say that no man had touched her save her husband and the beggar. The pain of their deceit caused the lovers to separate. They lived miserably without each other. Tristan married a woman with Iseult's name. He died of a broken heart upon hearing a false report of her death. Iseult lived in sorrow until she too died. Some commentators detect a Celtic motif in the tale. The goddess of sovereignty selects the king. No man can rule without her approval. The love triangle also appears in Ireland. Fionn mac Cumhaill's bride Gráinne eloped with Diarmaid. In the Irish tale the heroine is more active in the romance.
